title: Episode 141: Andrew Johnson and the Veto War: The Clash Over Reconstruction
description:
When Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, the daunting task of reconstructing a shattered Union fell to Andrew Johnson—a self-made tailor from East Tennessee who had never attended a single day of school. Johnson was a lifelong Southern Democrat and fierce Unionist who despised the planter aristocracy. Yet his stubborn obstinacy, rigid constitutional dogmatism, and deep racial prejudice soon ignited an unprecedented constitutional war with the Radical Republican majority in Congress. From his shocking vetoes of the Freedmen's Bureau and the Civil Rights Act of 1866 to his disastrous 'Swing Around the Circle' speaking tour, this is the story of how an unyielding president shattered national unity and provoked a historic congressional revolution.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the turbulent aftermath of the American Civil War, where the assassination of Abraham Lincoln thrust Andrew Johnson—a combative, illiterate runaway apprentice turned border-state senator—into the highest office in the land. Johnson's collision with Congress over the rights of four million newly emancipated citizens remains one of the most explosive chapters in American history. Here is George with the full story of Andrew Johnson and the Great Veto War.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TAILOR FROM GREENEVILLE
No American president ever rose from deeper poverty or more severe adversity than Andrew Johnson. Born in a drafty two-room shack in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1808, Johnson lost his father at the age of three when the elder Johnson died after rescuing two wealthy citizens from a swollen river. Impoverished and unable to afford schooling, Johnson was bound out as an indentured tailor's apprentice at age ten. Treated like an unpaid servant, the fiery teenager rebelled and ran away, prompting his master to publish a newspaper notice offering a ten-dollar reward for the return of his runaway apprentice. Eventually, Johnson packed his sewing needles, shears, and thimble into a cart and crossed the Great Smoky Mountains on foot, settling in the frontier town of Greeneville in East Tennessee.

In Greeneville, Johnson opened a tailoring shop that quickly became the town's informal political forum. While he sat cross-legged on his wooden workbench stitching coats and trousers, he paid local laborers to read aloud to him from speeches of British parliamentarians and the United States Constitution. At eighteen, he married Eliza McCardle, a local shoemaker's daughter who patiently taught him how to write and perform arithmetic. Blessed with a booming baritone voice and an electrifying, combative speaking style, Johnson emerged as the fierce champion of the plebeian mountain folk—the small non-slaveholding farmers, carpenters, and day laborers who harbored deep resentment against the arrogant, wealthy slaveholding plantation aristocracy of Middle and West Tennessee. He climbed the political ladder with relentless determination: alderman, mayor, state legislator, congressman, governor, and United States senator.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LONE SOUTHERN SENATOR AND THE KIRKWOOD HOUSE
In the winter of 1860, as the southern states seceded one by one following Lincoln's election, Andrew Johnson made the defining choice of his life. Speaking on the floor of the United States Senate while armed with a loaded pistol in his pocket for self-defense, Johnson denounced secession as treason and heresy. When Tennessee voted to leave the Union in June 1861, Johnson refused to resign his seat. He was the only sitting senator from any seceding state who remained loyal to the United States government. Confederate mobs burned him in effigy, confiscated his property in Greeneville, and forced his frail wife and children into hiding. In the North, Johnson was instantly hailed as a hero—a fearless, incorruptible patriot who put country above section.

In 1862, Lincoln appointed Johnson military governor of Tennessee, tasking him with the dangerous mission of pacifying a hostile civilian population and restoring federal authority under martial law. To broaden his appeal for the 1864 presidential election, Lincoln ran on a bipartisan National Union ticket and selected Johnson as his vice-presidential running mate. But the triumph began on a disastrous note. On March 4, 1865, suffering from severe typhoid fever, Johnson drank three glasses of whiskey in the Vice President's office to steady his nerves before delivering a rambling, slurred, and utterly incoherent inaugural speech to a horrified Senate. Six weeks later, on the morning of April 15, Lincoln lay dead at the Petersen House, and Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase administered the presidential oath to Andrew Johnson in his parlor at the Kirkwood House.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ILLUSION OF RETRIBUTION AND THE RISE OF THE BLACK CODES
When Johnson took the oath, the Radical Republicans in Congress rejoiced. They remembered Johnson's fiery wartime speeches in which he had repeatedly roared that 'treason must be made odious, and traitors must be punished and impoverished.' Men like Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts and Representative Thaddeus Stevens of Pennsylvania believed Johnson would be far tougher on the South than the merciful Lincoln. But the Radical leaders completely misunderstood Andrew Johnson's core political philosophy. Johnson was a Jacksonian states' rights Democrat through and through. He had hated the plantation lords because they were an arrogant economic oligarchy, not because he cared about the civil rights or citizenship of Black Americans. In Johnson's view, once the plantation barons were stripped of power and slavery was abolished, the rebellious states had never legally left the Union, and their internal affairs were none of the federal government's business.

Taking advantage of an eight-month congressional recess from April to December 1865, Johnson instituted his own program of Presidential Reconstruction. He offered broad amnesties and pardons to hundreds of thousands of former Confederates upon a simple oath of allegiance, personally signing thousands of special pardons for wealthy planters who flattered his vanity. Unchastened, white Southern political leaders quickly reasserted complete control over their state governments. They enacted the infamous 'Black Codes'—repressive statutes that barred African Americans from buying or renting land outside cities, subjected them to arrest for vagrancy if they were unemployed, forced them into coercive annual labor contracts on former plantations, and prohibited them from testifying against white persons in court or bearing arms. To Northern observers who had just buried hundreds of thousands of sons, it appeared that the South had surrendered on the battlefield only to restore slavery by law.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE VETO OF THE FREEDMEN'S BUREAU
When the Thirty-ninth Congress convened in Washington in December 1865, Northern senators and representatives were stunned to find their former Confederate enemies—including Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens, six Confederate cabinet members, four Confederate generals, and dozens of rebel colonels—arriving in Washington with fresh presidential pardons in hand, demanding to take their seats in Congress. Led by Thaddeus Stevens, the Republican majority refused to call the roll of Southern delegates, slamming the doors of Congress in their faces and creating a Joint Committee on Reconstruction to investigate conditions in the South.

Moderate Republicans, led by Senator Lyman Trumbull of Illinois, sought to avoid a breach with the President. In February 1866, Congress passed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill, expanding the federal agency created by Lincoln to provide food, medical aid, schools, and legal protection to four million freed slaves and displaced white refugees across the ruined South. To the shock and dismay of moderates, Johnson slapped the bill with a furious presidential veto. In his message, Johnson argued that the bureau was unconstitutional, too expensive, and created a dangerous system of federal dependency. Worse, he openly declared that Congress had no constitutional authority to pass laws affecting the southern states so long as eleven southern states were excluded from representation in the legislature. It was a direct challenge to the legitimacy of the United States Congress itself.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CIVIL RIGHTS ACT OF 1866: A CONSTITUTIONAL WATERSHED
Three weeks after his veto of the Freedmen's Bureau, Johnson escalated the fight into personal warfare. On Washington's Birthday, February 22, 1866, a crowd of supporters serenaded the President outside the White House. Giving in to his worst combative instincts, Johnson launched into a sixty-minute unscripted tirade. He accused Charles Sumner, Thaddeus Stevens, and Wendell Phillips of being traitors who were actively conspiring to destroy the Union and have him assassinated, just as Lincoln had been. Moderate Republicans who had sought a compromise were mortified; any hope of working with the executive vanished.

In March 1866, Congress responded by passing the landmark Civil Rights Act of 1866—the first major statutory guarantee of civil rights in American history. Drafted by Lyman Trumbull, the act declared that all persons born in the United States, without regard to race or color, were citizens of the United States, possessing full and equal benefit of all laws for the security of person and property. Once again, Johnson struck the legislation down with a vitriolic veto, claiming the bill unfairly discriminated against the white race in favor of the newly freed slaves. But this time, Congress had had enough. On April 9, 1866, for the first time in American history, both the House and the Senate mustered the necessary two-thirds majority to override a presidential veto on a major piece of legislation. Power in Washington decisively shifted from the Executive Mansion to Capitol Hill.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SWING AROUND THE CIRCLE
Determined to overturn the Republican majorities in the upcoming midterm elections of 1866, Andrew Johnson embarked on an unprecedented national speaking campaign known as the 'Swing Around the Circle.' No American president had ever openly campaigned across the country for congressional candidates. Accompanied by a reluctant General Ulysses S. Grant and Admiral David Farragut, Johnson boarded a private train that traveled through Philadelphia, New York, Buffalo, Cleveland, Chicago, St. Louis, and Indianapolis.

What was intended as a dignified presidential tour degenerated into an unmitigated public relations disaster. Across Ohio, Michigan, and Indiana, large, hostile crowds heckled the President, shouting insults, chanting the names of Lincoln and Grant, and holding up signs mocking his speeches. Instead of maintaining presidential dignity, Johnson lost his temper repeatedly. Standing on train platforms, his face flushed with rage, he traded screaming insults with hecklers. In Cleveland, when someone in the crowd shouted, 'Hang Jeff Davis!', Johnson bellowed back, 'Why not hang Thad Stevens and Wendell Phillips too?' In Indianapolis, a riot broke out between supporters and opponents, leaving one person dead and forcing Johnson to flee inside his hotel. General Grant was so disgusted by the spectacle that he faked illness to escape the train in St. Louis, privately writing to his wife that he was utterly ashamed to be associated with the President's undignified exhibition.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RECONSTRUCTION ACTS AND THE PATH TO CONFRONTATION
The voters rendered their verdict in the fall of 1866 with crushing finality. The Northern electorate overwhelmingly repudiated Andrew Johnson, handing the Republican Party veto-proof two-thirds supermajorities in both houses of Congress. With this mandate, the Radical and moderate Republicans seized total control of Reconstruction policy. When Southern legislatures, emboldened by Johnson, overwhelmingly rejected the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress dismantled Johnson's state governments entirely.

In March 1867, Congress passed the sweeping Military Reconstruction Acts over Johnson's vetoes. The South was carved into five military districts, each placed under the command of a federal army general backed by Union troops. To regain readmission to the Union and representation in Congress, Southern states were required to draft new state constitutions granting universal male suffrage to Black citizens and formally ratify the Fourteenth Amendment. Johnson used every executive power at his disposal to obstruct, delay, and undermine the enforcement of these laws, removing cooperative military commanders like Philip Sheridan and Daniel Sickles. Congress, realizing that the President would stop at nothing to sabotage federal law, decided to set a legal snare that would either break his executive power or drive him from office entirely. The stage was set for the first impeachment trial of an American president.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Andrew Johnson's bitter war against Congress transformed the nature of American Reconstruction, turning a fragile peace into an intractable ideological trench warfare. His unyielding refusal to compromise forged an unprecedented congressional coalition that permanently etched birthright citizenship and equal protection into the Constitution. Next week, we examine the explosive climax of this struggle: the Tenure of Office Act, the barricaded War Department, and the high-stakes Senate trial that came down to a single dramatic vote. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
